queue.title: AI Supplier Contracts
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses AI supplier contracts, key clauses, and practical consequences for data and model governance.

A standard software contract often doesn't cover the risks of a model, data, and variable AI results.

An AI service isn't just software. It includes a model that can change, data that can be used to improve the service, and a result whose accuracy depends on context.

The contract must clearly state whether the supplier may use input data for training, where data is processed, how an incident is reported, and what happens after the service ends.

A minimum level of documentation, notice of a material model change, and a way to verify a result affecting rights, finances, or contractual obligations must be defined.

This publication is an original analysis; the sources cited serve as reference documentation.

queue.title: Managing Cross-Border Projects: Accountability
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses cross-border project governance, key accountability practices, and practical consequences.

The project's central goal must remain unified, while local legal and operational controls must be clearly documented.

An international project fails when the central team assumes one operating model is automatically applicable in every country.

One person must be accountable for the result, but local owners are also needed for permits, taxes, labour relations, suppliers, and technical conditions.

Every deviation must be documented as a local control, not hidden in email exchanges or verbal agreements.

A unified goal and local demonstrability aren't opposites. Together they make a project scalable.

This publication is an original analysis; the sources cited serve as reference documentation.

queue.title: AI Must Not Write the Final Decision
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

A model can prepare a draft, but cannot take responsibility for a decision's consequence. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

A model can prepare a draft, but it cannot take responsibility for the consequence of a decision.

AI can find a pattern, summarise a document, and suggest text. That's useful, but it's not the same as making a decision. The final decision must remain with a person who understands the context, holds the authority, and can explain why a given result was accepted or rejected. An organisation that hides accountability behind a model isn't automating a process. It's automating an excuse.

This publication is an original analysis; the sources cited serve as reference documentation.

In practice, this means the accountable person must be able to reject a model's recommendation without justification, because that very ability to refuse is the proof that the decision genuinely belongs to a person, not the algorithm that proposed it.

The distinction matters most in edge cases, where a model's training data may not reflect a genuinely novel situation, and where a purely mechanical application of past patterns could produce a confidently wrong result. A human reviewer who understands this limitation, and who is empowered to override the model without needing to justify every override, is not a redundant layer of process — it is the mechanism by which the organisation catches the cases the model was never equipped to handle correctly.
